title: Glossary of 52 Key Words in 1 Peter
description: A practical dictionary for Bible study, written in simple language for everyone, from new believers to seasoned disciples. Each word is defined as Peter uses it in his first letter to the early Church.

glossary.definition: The Creator and Ruler of everything. In 1 Peter, God is not a distant force. He is a Father who loves, a Judge who is fair, and a Shepherd who cares. Peter keeps pointing us back to God as the center of everything: our suffering, our hope, our calling. When life gets hard, Peter says: look at God, not at your circumstances.
glossary.key_verse: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

glossary.definition: The title that means 'the Anointed One,' the promised Savior. Peter doesn't just talk about Christ as a historical figure. He presents Christ as someone who suffered for us, left us an example to follow, and who is coming back in glory. Christ is the foundation the whole letter stands on.
glossary.key_verse: Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God.

glossary.definition: Peter uses 'good' constantly. Good behavior, good works, good conscience, good days, the Good News. Why? Because the world was accusing Christians of being evildoers. Peter's answer is simple: let your life be so visibly good that even your enemies have to shut their mouths. Your good life is your loudest testimony.
glossary.key_verse: Having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God.

glossary.definition: The visible greatness and honor of God. In 1 Peter, glory is always the finish line. Suffering comes first, glory comes after. Peter saw Christ's suffering with his own eyes, and now he says: hold on, the glory is coming. Every trial you endure is preparing something eternal.
glossary.key_verse: But may the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.

glossary.definition: The personal name of the Son of God, meaning 'God saves.' Every time Peter says 'Jesus,' he's reminding us this isn't just theology. It's a real Person who walked, bled, died, and rose again. This is the Jesus that Peter denied three times, and the same Jesus who restored him. That's the beauty of it.
glossary.key_verse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

glossary.definition: Anything that opposes God's character and purposes. Peter is very practical here. Evil speaking, evil desires, doing evil, rendering evil for evil. He's not talking about some abstract concept. He's saying: when someone insults you, don't fire back. When the world does wrong, don't copy them. Break the cycle.
glossary.key_verse: Not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.

glossary.definition: The Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity. In 1 Peter, the Spirit is the one who sets us apart (sanctification), who inspired the prophets, and who rests on us when we suffer for Christ's name. The Spirit is not just power. He's a Person who walks with you through the fire.
glossary.key_verse: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.

glossary.definition: God's undeserved favor toward us. Grace is the fuel of this entire letter. Peter opens with it, closes with it, and says it should be multiplied in our lives. Grace doesn't mean God ignores our failures. It means He gives us what we could never earn: forgiveness, hope, and strength to keep going.
glossary.key_verse: But may the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little while, perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you.

glossary.definition: Set apart. Different from the world, belonging to God. Peter quotes directly from the Old Testament: 'Be holy, because I am holy.' This isn't about being perfect. It's about your direction. Are you moving toward God or away from Him? Holiness is simply living in a way that reflects who your Father is.
glossary.key_verse: But just as he who called you is holy, you yourselves also be holy in all of your behavior.

glossary.definition: Our human, mortal nature. Peter contrasts flesh with spirit throughout the letter. Flesh is temporary, like grass that withers. Christ suffered 'in the flesh' so that we could live 'in the spirit.' The point is not that your body is bad, but that your old sinful patterns must not control you anymore.
glossary.key_verse: Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind; for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin.

glossary.definition: A title of supreme authority. When Peter says 'Lord,' he means the one who has the final word over everything. Your life, your circumstances, your enemies. Peter tells us to 'sanctify the Lord God in your hearts,' which basically means: give Him the throne of your life. Make Him the Boss, not your fears.
glossary.key_verse: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you.

glossary.definition: The message of God, both the Scriptures and the Gospel. Peter says this Word is 'living and abiding.' It doesn't expire, it doesn't go out of style. Everything in this world fades like grass and flowers, but God's Word endures forever. It's the seed that gives you new life.
glossary.key_verse: Having been born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, through the word of God, which lives and remains forever.

glossary.definition: Trusting God when you can't see the full picture. Peter says faith is more valuable than gold, and gold is tested by fire, so don't be surprised when your faith gets tested too. The beauty is this: you love someone you've never physically seen (Jesus), and that faith will result in the salvation of your soul.
glossary.key_verse: Whom, not having known, you love. In him, though now you don't see him, yet believing, you rejoice greatly with joy that is unspeakable and full of glory.

glossary.definition: Of immense value. Peter uses this word carefully. The blood of Christ is precious, Christ as the living stone is precious, and a gentle spirit is precious in God's sight. The world measures value by money and status. Peter says: the things that matter most to God are invisible to the world's eyes.
glossary.key_verse: Come to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious.

glossary.definition: The deepest part of who you are, your inner self. Peter talks about the 'salvation of your souls,' purifying your souls, and entrusting your souls to God. Your soul is what God is after. It's not about outward religion. It's about what's happening inside you, in the place only God can see.
glossary.key_verse: Receiving the result of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

glossary.definition: Physical death and spiritual death. Peter speaks of Christ being raised 'from the dead,' which changes everything. He also mentions the Gospel being preached 'to the dead' and God judging 'the living and the dead.' Death is real, but it doesn't have the final word. The resurrection broke that power.
glossary.key_verse: Who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in God.

glossary.definition: The plural form, meaning many types of pain and hardship. Peter knows suffering personally. He watched Jesus suffer, and now he writes to believers going through persecution. His message is not 'avoid pain' but 'understand its purpose.' Christ's sufferings opened the door to glory, and yours connect you to His story.
glossary.key_verse: But because you are partakers of Christ's sufferings, rejoice, that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy.

glossary.definition: Both physical existence and the new spiritual life in Christ. Peter says we were rescued from a 'useless way of life' inherited from our ancestors. The old life was empty. The new life is purposeful, eternal, and shared with others ('joint heirs of the grace of life'). God didn't just save you. He gave you a completely new existence.
glossary.key_verse: He who would love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit.

glossary.definition: Without end. Eternal. Peter uses this word for two things: the Word of God that 'endures forever' and the glory and power that belong to God 'forever and ever.' In a world where everything breaks, rusts, and dies, 'forever' is the word that reminds you: what God builds doesn't collapse.
glossary.key_verse: But the Lord's word endures forever. This is the word of Good News which was preached to you.

glossary.definition: The collective identity of believers. Peter quotes the Old Testament to say: 'You were not a people, but now you are God's people.' That's your identity shift. You went from nobodies to somebodies, not because of what you did, but because God claimed you as His own family.
glossary.key_verse: In the past, you were not a people, but now are God's people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.

glossary.definition: Our failures and rebellions against God. Peter doesn't sugarcoat sin. Christ 'bore our sins in his body on the tree' so that we could die to those sins and live for what's right. Sin is serious. It cost the Son of God His life. But the good news is: the price has already been paid.
glossary.key_verse: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness.

glossary.definition: God's purpose and plan. Peter mentions 'the will of God' as the compass for the Christian life. When you suffer for doing good, that's God's will. Not punishment, but purpose. When you stop living for human desires and start living for God's plan, that's the turning point of your whole life.
glossary.key_verse: That you no longer should live the rest of your time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God.

glossary.definition: Strangers in a land that's not your home. Peter opens his letter addressing believers as 'foreigners in the Dispersion.' This is your identity as a Christian: you live in this world, but you don't belong to it. You're passing through. That's why the world feels uncomfortable sometimes. It's not your final destination.
glossary.key_verse: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion.

glossary.definition: God as our Dad. Peter calls God 'the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ' and reminds us that when we call on Him as Father, we should live with reverent respect. God is not a distant authority. He's a Father who loves His children. But He's also a Father who takes our growth seriously.
glossary.key_verse: If you call on him as Father, who without respect of persons judges according to each man's work, pass the time of your living as foreigners here in reverent fear.

glossary.definition: The blood of Christ, the price of our redemption. Peter makes it very clear: you weren't bought with money, silver, or gold. The cost was the precious blood of Jesus, like a perfect lamb without any defect. This is the most expensive transaction in history, and it was paid for you.
glossary.key_verse: Knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things like silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ.

glossary.definition: Inner calm and restored relationship with God. Peter opens and closes his letter with peace. It's not the absence of problems. It's the presence of God in the middle of problems. Peter greets them with 'peace be multiplied' and closes with 'peace be to all of you who are in Christ Jesus.'
glossary.key_verse: Grace to you and peace be multiplied.

glossary.definition: God's compassion toward those who don't deserve it. Peter says God's 'great mercy' caused us to be born again. Mercy is when God holds back the punishment you earned and gives you a fresh start instead. You were outside God's family. Now you're in. That's mercy.
glossary.key_verse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope.

glossary.definition: Something that cannot decay, rust, or be destroyed. Peter uses this word for three things: our inheritance in heaven, the seed of God's Word, and the inner beauty of a gentle spirit. Everything in this world breaks down. But what God gives you, your salvation, your new life, your eternal reward, is indestructible.
glossary.key_verse: To an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn't fade away, reserved in Heaven for you.

glossary.definition: Where God dwells, and where our real future is. Peter says our inheritance is 'reserved in heaven,' the Holy Spirit was 'sent out from heaven,' and Christ has 'gone into heaven' with all authority. Heaven isn't just where you go when you die. It's the command center of the universe, and your name is registered there.
glossary.key_verse: To an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn't fade away, reserved in Heaven for you.

glossary.definition: Being rescued from sin, death, and judgment. Peter describes salvation as something the prophets searched for, the angels wanted to understand, and believers receive through faith. It's past (you were saved), present (you are being saved), and future (ready to be revealed in the last time). Salvation is the whole package.
glossary.key_verse: Who by the power of God are guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.

glossary.definition: A symbol of what the world considers most valuable. Peter says your faith is worth more than gold, and gold eventually perishes, even when refined by fire. Also, you weren't redeemed with gold or silver. The point is: stop measuring your life by what the world values. God's economy works differently.
glossary.key_verse: That the proof of your faith, which is more precious than gold that perishes, even though it is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise, glory, and honor.

glossary.definition: The moment when something hidden is made visible. Peter talks about the 'revelation of Jesus Christ,' when He returns and everything becomes clear. Right now, you walk by faith. But a day is coming when faith turns to sight, and every trial you endured will make sense in His presence.
glossary.key_verse: Set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

glossary.definition: A picture of how short human life is. Peter quotes Isaiah: 'All flesh is like grass.' Beautiful today, gone tomorrow. This isn't meant to depress you. It's meant to redirect your priorities. Don't invest everything in what's temporary. The grass withers, but the Lord's word endures forever.
glossary.key_verse: All flesh is like grass, and all of man's glory like the flower in the grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls.

glossary.definition: Related to the Spirit and the inner life. Peter talks about 'pure spiritual milk' for growth, 'spiritual sacrifices' that please God, and being built into a 'spiritual house.' The Christian life is not only about outward behavior. It's about an invisible transformation happening inside you that changes everything on the outside.
glossary.key_verse: You also as living stones are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

glossary.definition: A title for Christ and an identity for believers. Jesus is the 'living stone' that builders rejected but God chose. And here's the incredible part: you are also living stones, being built into a spiritual house alongside Him. You're not random bricks. You're carefully placed by the Master Builder.
glossary.key_verse: Come to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious.

glossary.definition: Those who reject God's Word. Peter uses this word for people who stumble over the truth because they refuse to believe it. The stone that was meant to be their foundation becomes a 'stumbling stone' instead. Disobedience isn't just breaking rules. It's saying 'no' to the God who offers you life.
glossary.key_verse: For they stumble at the word, being disobedient, to which also they were appointed.

glossary.definition: Your inner sense of right and wrong before God. Peter says baptism is an 'appeal to God for a good conscience,' and he encourages keeping your conscience clean so that when people accuse you, they find nothing to stick. A clear conscience is your peace at night. You can sleep knowing you did what was right.
glossary.key_verse: Having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.

glossary.definition: Missing God's standard, falling short of who He made you to be. Peter says Christ 'didn't sin' (He's our example), that Christ 'suffered for sins once' (He's our substitute), and that we should 'cease from sin' (that's our calling). Sin is the disease. Christ is the cure. And the new life is the recovery.
glossary.key_verse: Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God.

glossary.definition: One who protects, feeds, and leads the flock. Peter calls Jesus 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls' and later 'the chief Shepherd.' Peter himself was told by Jesus: 'Feed my sheep.' A shepherd doesn't run when wolves come. He stays. That's what Jesus does for you. He stays.
glossary.key_verse: For you were going astray like sheep; but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

glossary.definition: Living in alignment with God's character. Peter says 'the righteous' person who suffers for doing right is blessed, that Christ (the righteous one) suffered for the unrighteous, and that God's eyes are on the righteous. Righteousness isn't perfection. It's direction. It's choosing God's way when the easy road pulls the other way.
glossary.key_verse: For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears open to their prayer.

glossary.definition: A word that means 'so be it' or 'this is true and final.' Peter uses it to seal his statements about God's glory and power. When you say 'Amen,' you're putting your signature on what God has declared. It's your 'yes' to His truth.
glossary.key_verse: To him be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.

glossary.definition: Christ rising from the dead, and the foundation of everything we believe. Without the resurrection, there's no living hope, no new birth, no future. Peter grounds the entire letter on this event: God 'caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.'
glossary.key_verse: This is a symbol of baptism, which now saves you... through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

glossary.definition: God's ability to accomplish His purposes. Peter says we are 'guarded by the power of God' through faith, and he closes the letter giving God all the 'power forever.' You are not holding on to God. God's power is holding on to you. That's the difference between religion and real faith.
glossary.key_verse: Who by the power of God are guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.

glossary.definition: Responding to God's truth with action, not just agreement. Peter talks about 'obedience to the truth' that purifies the soul and being 'children of obedience.' Real faith always produces obedience. Not forced, but willing. When you truly understand what God has done for you, obedience becomes your natural response.
glossary.key_verse: Seeing you have purified your souls in your obedience to the truth through the Spirit in sincere brotherly affection, love one another from the heart fervently.

glossary.definition: The present system that operates apart from God. Peter says Christ was 'foreknown before the foundation of the world' and that our brothers 'in the world' share our same sufferings. The world is not your enemy, but its values, priorities, and patterns are not your guide anymore. You answer to a different King.
glossary.key_verse: Who was foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in this last age for your sake.

glossary.definition: A symbol of beauty that fades quickly. Peter quotes Isaiah: 'man's glory is like the flower in the grass.' Status, achievements, physical beauty. They're real, but they don't last. The flower falls. Only what's rooted in God's Word survives the seasons.
glossary.key_verse: All flesh is like grass, and all of man's glory like the flower in the grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls.

glossary.definition: The collective identity of all believers as people who serve God directly. In the Old Testament, only certain people could approach God. Now, Peter says YOU are a 'holy priesthood' and a 'royal priesthood.' Every believer has direct access to God. You don't need a middle man. Christ already opened the door.
glossary.key_verse: You also as living stones are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

glossary.definition: The most important stone in a building, the one that determines the alignment of everything else. Christ is the 'chief cornerstone.' If your life is built on Him, everything else lines up. If it's built on anything else (money, relationships, reputation), it will eventually collapse.
glossary.key_verse: Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious. He who believes in him will not be disappointed.

glossary.definition: Enduring pain for doing what's right. Peter says it's 'better to suffer for doing what is right than for doing evil.' Suffering is not proof that God has abandoned you. In Peter's world, suffering is proof that you belong to Christ, because He suffered first, and He's walking through it with you.
glossary.key_verse: For it is better, if it is God's will, that you suffer for doing what is right than for doing evil.

glossary.definition: Fellow believers, your spiritual family. Peter talks about 'sincere brotherly affection' and knowing that your 'brothers in the world' share your same struggles. You are not alone in this. The Church is not a building. It's your brothers and sisters walking the same road, carrying each other through the hard seasons.
glossary.key_verse: Withstand him steadfast in your faith, knowing that your brothers who are in the world are undergoing the same sufferings.

glossary.definition: Putting God first and yourself last. Peter says to 'clothe yourselves with humility' like you'd put on a garment every morning. Why? Because 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.' Humility is not thinking less of yourself. It's thinking of yourself less. It's recognizing that God is God, and you are not.
glossary.key_verse: Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.'

glossary.definition: God's people, pictured as sheep under a shepherd's care. Peter tells the elders to 'shepherd the flock of God,' not by force, but willingly. And he reminds them that they should be examples, not bosses. The flock belongs to God, not to any leader. Leaders serve the flock; the flock follows the Chief Shepherd.
glossary.key_verse: Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not for dishonest gain, but willingly.

the_living_god.label: The Living God
the_living_god.description: Peter wrote this letter to people who were scared, scattered, and suffering. So the very first thing he does is point them to God. Not an idea about God, but the Living God Himself. A Father who chose them before the world began. A Son who bled for them and rose again. A Spirit who set them apart and walks with them through the fire. In 1 Peter, God is not watching from a distance. He is guarding your salvation, hearing your prayers, and holding your future in His hands. Every word in this category reveals a different side of who He is, and the more you know Him, the less you fear everything else.
the_living_god.source_verse: 1 Peter 1:3, 'the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ'

the_precious_blood.label: The Precious Blood
the_precious_blood.description: This is the price tag of your freedom. Peter tells his readers: you were stuck in an empty way of life inherited from your parents, and no amount of money could buy you out. What set you free was something the world can't put a number on: the precious blood of Christ, like a perfect lamb without a single defect. Everything in this category flows from that one sacrifice: grace, mercy, salvation, resurrection, heaven, peace. These are not things you earned. They are gifts purchased at the highest cost in the history of the universe. Peter wants you to understand the weight of what was paid so that you never take lightly what you've received.
the_precious_blood.source_verse: 1 Peter 1:19, 'precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish'

the_royal_priesthood.label: The Royal Priesthood
the_royal_priesthood.description: This is your new identity. Before Christ, you were not a people. Now you are God's people. Before mercy, you had no access to God. Now you are a holy priesthood with a direct line to the throne. Peter spends a large part of his letter telling believers who they are and how that identity should shape the way they live. You are foreigners in this world, yes, but you are also a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. The words in this category describe your calling: faith, obedience, humility, good conscience, brotherhood. This is not about religion. This is about becoming the person God already declared you to be.
the_royal_priesthood.source_verse: 1 Peter 2:9, 'a royal priesthood, a holy nation'

the_fiery_trial.label: The Fiery Trial
the_fiery_trial.description: Peter does not sugarcoat reality. He tells you straight: suffering is coming, and it's not an accident. The fiery trial is real. Persecution, temptation, the pull of your old life, the weight of living in a world that doesn't understand you. But here's what makes 1 Peter different from a pessimistic letter: the fire has a purpose. Gold is tested by fire to prove it's real. Your faith is tested the same way. Every word in this category (evil, flesh, sin, suffering, death) is something Christ already defeated. The fire is not the end of the story. It's the road from the cross to the crown.
the_fiery_trial.source_verse: 1 Peter 4:12, 'don't be astonished at the fiery trial'
